title: Elements and compounds
competency: Differentiate elements and compounds, and classify elements as metals and non-metals.

keywords.def: A pure substance that cannot be broken down into simpler substances by ordinary chemical means.
The smallest particle of an element.
An element that is shiny, conducts heat and electricity, and is malleable and ductile.
An element without metallic properties: dull and a poor conductor.
Can be drawn into thin wire.
A pure substance made of more than one type of atom bonded together.
A compound formed from two different elements, like sodium chloride.

en.text: An element is a pure substance that cannot be broken down into simpler substances by ordinary chemical means. It has only one kind of atom. 118 elements are known; 92 occur naturally. Metals like gold, iron and copper are shiny, conduct heat and electricity, and are malleable and ductile. Non-metals like carbon, oxygen and sulfur are dull and poor conductors.

screens.title: Why copper?
screens.ask: Electric wires are made of copper, not sulfur. Why?
screens.after: Copper is a metal: a good conductor and it can be drawn into wire. Sulfur is a non-metal and does not conduct.

screens.title: 2.3.2 Elements
paras: An element is a pure substance that cannot be broken down by ordinary chemical means.
It has only one kind of particle, the atom.
At present 118 elements are known. 92 occur naturally on Earth.
Elements are divided into metals and non-metals.

screens.title: Metals
paras: Examples: gold, iron, silver, copper, aluminium, sodium, lead.
They are shiny (lustrous).
They are good conductors of heat and electricity.
Most have high density and high melting points.
They are malleable and ductile.
They are solid at room temperature, except mercury, a liquid.

screens.title: Non-metals
paras: Examples: carbon, oxygen, sulfur, fluorine, phosphorus.
They are dull and do not conduct heat or electricity.
They have low melting and boiling points.
Bromine is a liquid at room temperature.

screens.title: Table 2.3 Metals and non-metals
table: Solid at room temperature, except mercury
Exist as solids, liquids and gases
Very hard, except sodium and potassium

screens.title: Key words
defs: A pure substance that cannot be broken down into simpler substances by ordinary chemical means.
The smallest particle of an element.
An element that is shiny, conducts heat and electricity, and is malleable and ductile.
An element without metallic properties: dull and a poor conductor.
Can be drawn into thin wire.

screens.text: Which element is a liquid metal at room temperature?
screens.why: Metals are solid at room temperature except mercury. Bromine is liquid but a non-metal.
Use the examples in the book.
screens.clue: Is it shiny and a good conductor?

screens.text: Substance Y is a hard, shiny solid that conducts heat and electricity well. Y is likely a …
screens.why: Shiny, hard and conducting: metal properties.

screens.ask: A metal that can be hammered into thin sheets is called ___.
screens.why: Malleability is being pressed into sheets.

screens.text: Which non-metal is essential for our life because we breathe it?
screens.why: We need oxygen to breathe and release energy from food. Iron is a metal.
screens.clue: Which non-metal is in the air we breathe?

en.text: A compound is a pure substance made of more than one type of atom bonded together. It can be broken into its elements only by chemical means. Water breaks into hydrogen and oxygen with electricity. Sodium chloride is made of sodium and chlorine. A compound's properties differ from those of its elements.

screens.title: Iron + sulfur
screens.ask: Iron filings are mixed with sulfur. A magnet still pulls the iron out. After strong heating, the magnet no longer does. What happened?
opts: A new substance, a compound, formed
screens.after: Heating joined iron and sulfur chemically into iron sulfide, a compound with new properties.

screens.title: Compounds
paras: A compound is a pure substance made of more than one type of atom bonded together.
It can be broken into two or more elements by chemical means.
Electric current breaks water into hydrogen and oxygen.
Sodium chloride forms from sodium and chlorine.
A compound of two different elements is a binary compound.

screens.title: What distinguishes an element from a compound?
paras: A compound's properties are different from those of its elements.
In a compound the elements are chemically, not physically, combined.

screens.title: Experiment 2.2 Distinguishing compounds and mixtures
steps: Part I: mix 7 g iron powder with 4 g sulfur powder. The mixture is grey with yellow and black grains.
A magnet pulls the iron out. A mixture can be separated physically.
Part II (teacher demonstration, ventilated room): heat 2 g of mixture until it glows orange.
The glow spreads through the mixture by itself.
The product, iron(II) sulfide, is a black solid. A magnet does not pick it up.
A new substance with new properties formed: a compound.

screens.title: Key words
defs: A pure substance made of more than one type of atom bonded together.
A compound formed from two different elements, like sodium chloride.

screens.text: How can water be broken into hydrogen and oxygen?
screens.why: A compound is broken into its elements only by chemical means.
screens.clue: Physical methods cannot split a compound.

screens.why: Compounds contain more than one type of atom.
screens.clue: Is it made of one kind of atom?

screens.text: Sodium chloride has the same properties as sodium and chlorine.
screens.why: A compound's properties differ from those of its elements.
screens.clue: Do we eat chlorine gas? We eat table salt.

screens.text: Magnesium filings and sulfur are put in a beaker, then heated so they react to form magnesium sulfide. What is it before and after?
screens.why: Before heating they are only placed together: a mixture. The reaction joins them chemically into a new compound.

items.text: What do you observe as you bring the magnet close to the iron–sulfur mixture?
opts: The iron filings stick to the magnet; the sulfur stays
items.ans: The iron filings stick to the magnet; the sulfur stays
items.why: Iron is magnetic, sulfur is not. In a mixture each keeps its properties.

items.text: What do you see under the magnifying glass?
opts: Separate grains of grey iron and yellow sulfur
items.ans: Separate grains of grey iron and yellow sulfur
items.why: In a mixture the particles are not joined.
items.clue: Is it still a mixture in Part I?

items.text: After heating (Part II), the black product is not attracted by a magnet. Why?
opts: A new compound, iron(II) sulfide, formed
items.ans: A new compound, iron(II) sulfide, formed
items.why: A compound has properties different from its elements.

test.why: Iron has only one kind of atom.

test.text: Metals are good conductors of heat and electricity.
test.why: That is a property of metals.

test.text: A compound can be broken into its elements by …
test.why: Only chemical means split a compound.

test.text: Ductility means a metal can be …
test.why: Ductile: drawn into wire. Malleable: hammered into sheets.

notes.text: Experiment 2.2 Part II is a teacher demonstration. Heating sulfur can give off toxic sulfur dioxide: do it in a ventilated room or fume cupboard, with eye protection.
Table 2.3 says non-metals are dull "except iodine"; graphite (carbon) is also shiny and conducts. The lesson does not say "only iodine".
